title: Fishermen, Outcasts and New Wine
overview: Jesus calls his first close followers, heals people others kept at a distance, and faces growing questions from religious experts about his authority and the company he keeps.

parts.label: A huge catch of fish (vv. 1-11)
parts.note: After a fruitless night of fishing, Simon Peter lets down his nets again only because Jesus asks, and the catch nearly sinks two boats. Peter's plea for Jesus to leave him is not rejection but a feeling of being unworthy before such power, and Jesus answers by turning his trade into a picture of his new work: gathering people instead of fish.

parts.label: Touching a man with leprosy (vv. 12-16)
parts.note: The word translated leprosy then covered various skin diseases that made a person ritually unclean, cut off from community and worship, so Jesus touching him was startling. Sending him to the priest followed the law of Moses for being officially declared clean and welcomed back into ordinary life.

parts.label: Through the roof (vv. 17-26)
parts.note: Friends lower a paralyzed man through a flat tiled roof, and Jesus tells him his sins are forgiven, which the religious experts see as blasphemy, claiming a right that belongs to God alone. Jesus, using his favorite title for himself, the Son of Man, heals the man as visible proof that he has that authority.

parts.label: Dinner with tax collectors (vv. 27-32)
parts.note: Tax collectors gathered money for Rome or its local rulers, often overcharged, and were widely despised as collaborators and cheats. Jesus calls one of them, Levi, and eats with his friends, explaining that a doctor is for the sick, not the healthy.

parts.label: Fasting and new wine (vv. 33-39)
parts.note: Jesus compares his time with his followers to a wedding, where guests celebrate rather than go without food, and Christians read the bridegroom's removal as a hint at his coming death. The patch and wineskin sayings suggest his message will not fit old patterns, and the final line about preferring old wine seems to admit that people often resist something new, though its exact point is debated.

think: Peter's first reaction to something overwhelming was to feel he did not belong there; when have you felt out of your depth like that, and what did you do with the feeling?
